fr:mainmatter.fr:p: This note expands the ISA-level sketch on LC3 in Lean

The machine is a 16-bit word architecture with 2^{16} addresses. In Lean, memory is a fixed-length array of UInt16 values indexed by addresses of the same width (LC3Lean/Memory.lean: MEMORY_MAX, read, write). There is no paging or protection: every address names a word of RAM, including the regions where trap vectors and memory-mapped devices live in ordinary LC-3 systems.

Programs are loaded from .obj files in Main.lean: the first big-endian 16-bit word is the load origin; subsequent byte pairs become successive words starting at that address. After loading, execution begins with the initial register state from Registers.init—notably the program counter starts at 0x3000, leaving lower addresses for trap-vector tables and OS conventions as in typical LC-3 coursework.

General-purpose registers R0–R7 are stored as an eight-element array. The program counter and condition code live beside them in Registers.Register: pc is a UInt16, and cond is exactly one of N, Z, or P. Helper set_condition_codes (Execution.lean) follows the usual LC-3 rule: after an instruction writes a value into a destination register, the flags reflect whether that value is negative (high bit set), zero, or strictly positive. LEA updates flags from the computed address; pure stores leave registers (and thus flags) unchanged.

Registers.read and Registers.write mediate access by register index; indices outside the LC-3 register file yield none, which propagates as failed execution steps—so the executable semantics are partial in exactly the places bad encodings would be nonsensical.

Each executed word is treated as an unsigned 16-bit instruction. The top four bits select the major opcode; instr_to_op in Instructions.lean maps that nybble to an Opcodes variant. Fields such as destination register DR, source registers SR1/SR2, base registers, and immediate bits are extracted with shifts and masks inside the per-opcode functions in Execution.lean, matching the bit layouts in the ISA sheet linked above.
Signed immediates use sign_extend with the appropriate width (imm5, imm6, PCoffset9, PCoffset11, etc.). Arithmetic is 16-bit modular arithmetic on UInt16 as in the reference VM narrative.

Sixteen opcode slots appear in the decoder, but two are deliberately non-executing in this codebase: OP_RTI and OP_RES map to op_rti and op_res, which return none (Execution.lean), so no architectural transition is defined for them here. The remaining fourteen correspond to the usual LC-3 instruction families:
Data movement and addressing: LD, LDI, LDR, LEA load a register from PC-relative, indirect, base-plus-offset, or “effective address” forms; ST, STI, STR store a register through the analogous addressing modes.
Arithmetic / logical: ADD and AND each choose either a second register or a sign-extended five-bit immediate; NOT bitwise complements a source into a destination.
Control flow: BR tests the nzp mask against the current condition code and optionally adds a PC-relative offset; JMP loads the PC from a base register (so RET is JMP R7 when conventions demand); JSR/JSRR save the linking address in R7 and jump either PC-relative or through a base register.
Traps: TRAP saves the link address in R7, loads the PC from the word at the trap vector address given by the low byte of the instruction, and falls through to whatever code lives there—in the pure executor this is exactly the ISA table lookup (op_trap); the interactive runner additionally recognizes the standard supervisor vectors and implements them natively (below). Each handler’s memory accesses and register updates are localized in op_*; comparing a handler to the ISA PDF row-by-row is the fastest way to see the precise semantics.

execute_step (Execution.lean) is the cycle spelled out in comments: read mem[pc]; advance pc by one; decode the opcode; run the selected op_*; return the updated register file and memory. Branches and jumps overwrite pc after that increment, which is the standard “PC points at next instruction unless the opcode replaces it” pattern. Trap setup writes R7 using the post-increment PC so the link register points after the TRAP word.

The LC-3 defines fixed eight-bit trap vectors (for example GETC = x20, OUT = x21, PUTS = x22, IN = x23, PUTSP = x24, HALT = x25). Execution.op_trap performs the generic ISA step: link in R7, pc ← mem[vector]. In the full interactive VM (Main.lean), once the opcode is recognized as TRAP, those six vectors are intercepted: after emulating the link behavior, control passes to Trap.op_trap_io, which implements PUTS, GETC, OUT, IN, PUTSP, and HALT using Lean IO and the terminal helpers—printing NUL-terminated word strings, packed byte strings, character I/O, and halting the loop—rather than executing whatever might reside in low memory for those vectors on bare metal.

That split matters for reading the repo: pure instruction semantics and proofs (LC3Correct) center on Execution.lean; observable terminal behavior additionally depends on Main.lean, Trap.lean, and the small POSIX terminal layer (c/terminal.c) used for raw mode and non-blocking keyboard checks.

Keyboard status and data follow the usual LC-3 addresses KBSR = xFE00 and KBDR = xFE02 (Main.lean). Loads that resolve to those addresses go through mem_read_io: a pending-key reference buffers one character so repeated status reads stay coherent, KBSR exposes the ready bit when input exists, and reading KBDR consumes the pending key. Only load paths are specialized in execute_step_io; other instructions reuse the pure functions from Execution.lean.

This page stays on the operational ISA story; the corresponding proof artifacts live under LC3Correct/, especially ExecutionCorrect.lean, with register and memory lemmas factoring out the boring consistency checks. If a statement here matches how you read the ISA PDF, the Lean theorems are the machine-checked version of that reading; if something diverges, trust the definitions you find in LC3Lean and the theorem statements they imply.

fr:title.text: Details on the Proofs of Correctness for LC3-Lean

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Details on the Proofs of Correctness for LC3-Lean

fr:mainmatter.fr:p: This note expands the proof sketch on LC3 in Lean into a reader’s guide to the LC3-Lean verification layer. The operational behavior of the machine—and how it maps to source files—is spelled out on the ISA-level companion page; here the focus is what Lean actually proves, how those statements are shaped, and what sits outside the proof footprint.

The proofs do not assert that “the VM feels like LC-3” in an informal sense. They assert precise implications about the pure Lean functions in LC3Lean/Execution.lean. For each implemented opcode handler op_*, there is a matching theorem op_*_spec in LC3Correct/ExecutionCorrect.lean. Each theorem has the same skeleton: case-split on the result of op_* instr reg mem. If the handler returns none, the conclusion is trivially true—no claim is made about stuck or malformed situations. If it returns some (reg', mem'), the conclusion spells out register and memory updates in terms of the instruction bits (DR, SR1, immediates, PC-relative offsets, and so on), Memory.read and Memory.write, Registers.read and Registers.write, and set_condition_codes.

Read that way, the specification is the structured postcondition inside each op_*_spec theorem: it is not a separate Coq-style module pretending to be “the ISA,” but a declarative description of what op_* does whenever it succeeds—written tightly enough that you can compare it line-by-line with the LC-3 instruction descriptions (for example in lc3-isa.pdf) and with the executable code.

ExecutionCorrect.lean contains one specification section per implemented handler. Together they cover the fourteen executing opcodes discussed on the ISA page: ADD, AND, BR, JMP, JSR, LD, LDI, LDR, LEA, NOT, ST, STI, STR, and TRAP. The decoder slots OP_RTI and OP_RES are handled in code by op_rti/op_res, which always return none; there are no corresponding op_*_spec theorems, because there is no successful transition to characterize.

Illustrative patterns (open ExecutionCorrect.lean for the full formulas): arithmetic and bitwise instructions relate the written value to register operands or sign-extended immediates and require reg' to come from set_condition_codes after the write. Loads and LEA tie the loaded or computed word to the addressing mode (PC + offset, mem[PC + offset], base-plus-offset, etc.) and again fix the flags from that result. Stores constrain mem' to a single Memory.write at the resolved address while leaving reg unchanged. BR distinguishes taken versus fall-through updates to pc; JMP and JSR relate pc (and R7 for linkage) to base registers or offsets decoded from the word. TRAP states that memory is unchanged, that R7 receives the current pc from the handler’s input state (which, in the full cycle, is already the post-fetch PC—see execute_step), and that the new pc is Memory.read mem trap_vector for the eight-bit trap vector field.

Two small libraries isolate facts the opcode proofs rely on without cluttering every tactic block:
LC3Correct/RegisterLemmas.lean proves that reads and writes on general-purpose indices 0–7 always succeed for well-formed register files, and that reading after writing the same index yields the value just written.
LC3Correct/MemoryLemmas.lean proves that every UInt16 address is within the array bounds implied by Memory.data_size, and standard single-address read/write consistency (read after write at the same address; stability at other addresses). Those lemmas formalize the mundane “array model actually behaves like memory” obligations so ExecutionCorrect can focus on instruction semantics.
fr:mainmatter.fr:em: Trust base and what is not covered
fr:mainmatter.fr:p: Lean itself is the proof checker: if lake build LC3Correct succeeds with no sorry, every theorem in that package is accepted by the kernel from the given definitions. The mathematical meaning is only as good as those definitions—which are intentionally shared with the simulator (LC3Lean imports).

What this stack does not currently bundle into a single end-to-end theorem: a wholesale specification of execute_step or of the Main loop including execute_step_io, trap interception, .obj loading, or the POSIX terminal FFI (c/terminal.c). The verified slice is the pure per-opcode semantics in Execution.lean (plus the register/memory infrastructure lemmas). Readers who want to extend assurance—for example a theorem threading fetch/decode around op_*_spec—would build on the same files but that composition is not what the existing lemmas headline.

For instruction-by-instruction intuition tied to addresses and traps, keep the ISA companion open beside ExecutionCorrect.lean; the former explains where Main diverges for real I/O, while the latter states exactly what Lean has checked about the pure core.
I recently implemented a formally verified virtual machine in Lean on which you can run 2048 in terminal! Try it out!

The LC-3 is a small 16-bit instructional architecture: eight general-purpose registers, a program counter, condition flags, and a 2^{16}-word address space. At each step the machine fetches a word from memory at the PC, decodes it as one of fourteen opcodes (from arithmetic and bitwise operations to loads, stores, branches, jumps, and subroutine calls), then updates registers, memory, and control flow accordingly. Beyond those opcodes, LC-3 programs rely on trap routines for console I/O and on memory-mapped I/O for the keyboard—so a faithful simulator must implement both the core instructions and this I/O story. For more on the architecture, see here.

The code in LC3-Lean is laid out as follows:
register and flag state lives in LC3Lean/Registers.lean,
the flat memory model in LC3Lean/Memory.lean,
opcode decoding in LC3Lean/Instructions.lean,
the fetch–decode–execute step and per-opcode semantics in LC3Lean/Execution.lean,
The runnable binary wires together loading of .obj files, the execution loop, and MMIO in Main.lean. If you open those modules, every informal claim in this paragraph—word size, register count, opcode coverage, traps, MMIO—is meant to be visible as definitions and executable code rather than hand-waving. The runnable binary wires together loading of .obj files, the execution loop, and MMIO in Main.lean.
For full details, see this page.

"Formally verified" here means that Lean checks mathematical theorems relating the implementation above to an explicit ISA-level specification of how each instruction may read and write registers and memory. Those theorems are stated and proved in the LC3Correct package—especially LC3Correct/ExecutionCorrect.lean, with supporting lemmas about registers and memory in LC3Correct/RegisterLemmas.lean and LC3Correct/MemoryLemmas.lean. Together they aim to capture, opcode by opcode, that the Lean executor’s effect on machine state matches the spec encoded alongside it. All proofs pass without sorry!

The boundary worth keeping in mind is the thin C shim (c/terminal.c) used for POSIX terminal raw mode and polling: it affects how characters reach your screen and keyboard, but the LC-3 machine semantics and the correctness proofs live on the Lean side. Readers who want the precise logical statement for a single opcode should start from LC3Correct/ExecutionCorrect.lean and follow the definitions it references—the prose here is only a map to those lemmas.
For full details, see this page.
